name: Karl Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Greenhill by half six. It's beef and wheat, about 120 suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves, and 300 hectares of grain. Tom Bauer owns it, and I feed the cattle, bed them down with straw and drive the tractor when he lets me. I've been there eighteen months, so I'm the new man, even with grey hair.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-two years driving lorries, mostly long distance, fridge trailers full of lettuce and yoghurt. My back gave out at 55 and the doctor said no more twelve-hour days in a cab. Tom's a friend of my brother-in-law and needed a pair of hands. The cattle don't talk back and the pay's good, so I've no complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, so nothing happens, good. I'm not one for big talk at the pub. Somebody'd bring it up and I'd say, told you, and order another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing until I stop, which is all I'm after. I don't use any of that stuff, never have. My phone does calls and the weather, and that's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Feed the cattle, drive the tractor, and Anna and I keep putting money aside like always. We'd keep the plan to finish at 65 and maybe get a little caravan by the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine. Nothing to feel, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any AI or smart kit on the farm already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's tractor has one of those GPS steering things, it drives itself in straight lines. He switches it on for me when we're drilling and I just sit there and turn at the ends. That's about as far as I go with the new stuff, and I don't ask how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever want to learn more about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not 30. I've got seven years left at most, if my back holds. Learning a computer now is like learning the violin, it's not going to pay off.

S0.say: I'd say right, so nothing happens, good. I'm not one for big talk at the pub; I'd say told you, and order another.
S0.think: It means I keep doing what I'm doing until I stop, which is all I'm after. My phone does calls and the weather, and that's plenty.
S0.do: Carries on feeding cattle and driving the tractor, and keeps saving with his wife as always. Keeps the plan to stop at 65 and buy a small caravan by the coast.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing much to feel about it.
S0.quote: Learning a computer now is like learning the violin, it's not going to pay off.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is a man of few words who measures everything against his remaining working years. He already sits in a self-steering tractor without wanting to know how it works. His reluctance is a plain cost-benefit judgement, not fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, they'll do what pays, they always have. When I was driving, the firm brought in trackers and cameras in every cab, and nobody asked us. You moan, you get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit worried, because I'm not quick. If Tom gets a robot that feeds the cattle and beds them down, what's left for me is the tractor, and the tractor drives itself already. I'd be the man sat in the cab for show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work well, and wait to see what Tom actually buys. If he wanted me to learn a feeding robot I'd try, but I'd not volunteer. We'd keep saving, and if it went bad I'd go to one of the other farms, there's always somebody short of hands round us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a funny knock in the engine on a long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture Tom telling you he's bought a feeding robot. What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, I'd sort of had a feeling. Then I'd ask how long I've got and whether there's a bit of money for going. I've done the sums. With what we got from selling the flat, we could stop at 61 if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take it personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. Eighteen months isn't long enough to make friends with a job. If I lost it I'd miss the cattle, they're good company, but I'm not going to lie awake over a job I've had less time than my car.

S1.say: I'd say it's business, and they'll do what pays, like they always have. When the haulage firm put cameras in every cab nobody asked us either; you moan and get on with it.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried because I'm not quick. If the owner buys a feeding robot, all that's left is the tractor, and that drives itself already.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and waits to see what the owner buys, trying a feeding robot only if asked. Keeps saving, and would move to another farm short of hands if the job went, knowing he could stop at 61 on savings from the sold flat.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a funny knock in the engine on a long run.
S1.quote: I'd be the man sat in the cab for show.
S1.fieldNote: He blames nobody: in his view it's just business, as with the trackers in his old lorries. His calm comes from having done the sums. He doesn't see his job as part of who he is yet, so losing it would sting but not break him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, two years, how's anybody meant to sort that out. I'd say it to Tom, to my brother-in-law, to the lads at the darts. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want to know what the government's doing, because it'd be a lot of people at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be gone from Greenhill by 60, and there'd be no other farm to go to, because they'd all have the same robots. Money-wise we'd scrape by fine till the pension. It's the sitting at home that'd get me. I've worked since I was sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd tell Anna we're cancelling the caravan and keeping that money in the bank. I'd ask Tom straight out what his plans are, and if he's buying, I'd ask for a few months' notice and some money for going. Once it hits, I'd stop, I suppose, and live off savings till the pension comes, and do up the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared about the money. Scared of the days being empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years of warning. What does that short a window change for you, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. With ten years I'd be out anyway. With two I'm pushed out at 60, which is five years early, and I'd be bored stiff and under Anna's feet. She's still at the school office, she'd come home and I'd have reorganised the kitchen again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in the family would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son, Diego. He's a mechanic at a garage in town, fixing cars. If robots are doing the driving and the fixing, what's he going to do at 33 with two little ones? I'd tell him not to buy the bigger house he's been looking at, not yet.

S2.say: I'd say two years is mad and ask how anybody's meant to sort it out. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want to know what the government's doing about so many people at once.
S2.think: I'd be gone by 60 with no other farm to go to, because they'd all have robots. Money would be fine till the pension; it's sitting at home that would get me.
S2.do: Cancels the caravan and keeps that money in the bank. Asks the owner straight out about his plans and for notice and a leaving payment, then stops work and lives on savings until his pension, and tells his son not to buy a bigger house yet.
S2.feel: Anxious, not about money but about empty days.
S2.quote: She's still at the school office, she'd come home and I'd have reorganised the kitchen again.
S2.fieldNote: His fear is idleness, not poverty: he has worked since sixteen. The two-year window pushes him out five years early, which is the real cost for him. His worry for his son, a mechanic with young children, is where the money concern shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is quick but not mad, so they'd better use it. I'd say it at the darts, and I'd say the young ones should be thinking about it. Me, I'd say I'll be sorted, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, at 63 I'd only be losing a couple of years. My back might decide that for me first anyway. So I'd be uneasy for the young lads more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Greenhill as long as Tom wanted me, and not change much. We'd keep saving, maybe a bit harder, and hold off on the caravan for a couple of years until we see. I'd have a word with Diego about putting money by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it'd be in the back of my head every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd see it coming for a few years. What would you do in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same as you'd do with a lorry nearing the end of its life. You keep running it, you don't put a new engine in it, and you put money aside for the next one. I'm the lorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot. Learning a robot at 61 for two years of work? No. If Tom said learn it or go, I'd likely go.

S3.say: I'd say five years is quick but not mad, so they'd better use it. The young ones should be thinking about it; I'd say I'll be sorted, more or less.
S3.think: At 63 I'd only lose a couple of years, and my back might decide that first anyway. I'd be uneasy for the young lads more than for myself.
S3.do: Keeps working at the farm as long as the owner wants him and saves a little harder. Puts the caravan on hold for a couple of years and talks to his son about putting money aside; would leave rather than learn a robot.
S3.feel: Uneasy, not losing sleep but thinking of it every morning.
S3.quote: You keep running it, you don't put a new engine in it, and you put money aside for the next one. I'm the lorry.
S3.fieldNote: His lorry comparison sums up how he sees himself: near the end, not worth new investment. With five years the gap between AGI and his planned exit shrinks enough to settle him. He would rather leave than learn at 61.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's ten years, plenty of time. I'd tell the young ones to get thinking. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch me. I'd be 68, retired, with a caravan if I'm lucky. I'd think about Diego and the grandkids, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am and finish at 65 like we planned. Buy the caravan. Tell Diego to start learning whatever the new car repair is going to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's somebody else's problem by then, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really push Diego to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, though I'd say it once, not every Sunday. He's a grown man. I'd say, look at what happened to lorry drivers with all the tracking and the automatic gearboxes, and get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you believe it would happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. I've heard a lot of big promises in my time. The self-driving lorries were meant to be here ten years ago and I never saw one on the motorway.

S4.say: I'd say that's ten years, plenty of time. I'd tell the young ones to get thinking and leave it at that.
S4.think: It doesn't touch me, because I'd be 68 and retired. I'd think about my son and the grandchildren, that's all.
S4.do: Carries on exactly as he is, finishes at 65 as planned and buys the caravan. Tells his son once to start learning whatever car repair becomes.
S4.feel: Calm, seeing it as mostly someone else's problem by then.
S4.quote: The self-driving lorries were meant to be here ten years ago and I never saw one on the motorway.
S4.fieldNote: The long window lands after his planned retirement, so he barely reacts. His doubt comes from his own trade's broken promises. He is careful not to nag his grown son.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for the money, we'd be all right. For being pushed out with no say and nothing to do, and for Diego with his little ones. What'd help is fair notice and a bit of money from the boss, and some sort of help for people like Diego, maybe paid retraining, so he's not stuck at 33.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I like the job. I do. I thought farming was going to be a step down after the lorries, and it's the best job I've had. Nobody's ever told me I'm late for a cow.

headlineQuote: Nobody's ever told me I'm late for a cow.
portrait: Karl Lopez is 58 and spent 32 years driving lorries until his back forced him off the road; for eighteen months he's fed cattle and driven the tractor at Greenhill, a beef and wheat farm. He's a man of few words who never uses AI and sees most change as just business. With savings from selling a flat, money barely worries him; what he fears is being pushed out early to empty days. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, mostly about idleness and his son, a mechanic with young children. With five or ten years he expects to reach retirement first and stays calm.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd be pushed out with no say and nothing to do, and his son would be stuck.
whatWouldHelp: Fair notice and a leaving payment from his boss, and paid retraining for younger people like his son.
